newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US, slumps vs mark on wobbly EMU.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US, slumps vs mark on wobbly EMU.

text.p: The dollar fell to a two-week low against the German mark as investors dumped most European currencies in favor of the relative safety of the German unit.

Various reports of weakening European resolve to cut bloated government spending in order to unite under a single currency triggered waves of mark buying, both against European units and the dollar, market players said.
"There seemed to have been great demand for marks," said Jay Wertheimer, senior foreign exchange trader at Banco di Sicilia in New York.

The dollar ended at 1.6980/85 marks, down from 1.7030/40 at the open and 1.7115/20 at Friday's close. But against the yen the greenback cut overnight losses to close at 125.32/37, up from 125.18/28 at the open, but down from 125.84/89 Friday.

A surprise announcement that France would hold parliamentary elections at the end of May cast doubts on France's commitment to slashing its goverment debt in preparation for a proposed single European currency in 1999.
French President Jacques Chirac announced the election at 1400 EDT/1900 GMT, stressing the need to strengthen France's position prior to European Economic and Monetary Union.
Chirac's decision was leaked overnight and the market failed to react to the announcement. But mark/Paris rallied sharply overnight, pressuring dollar/mark for the remainder of the session.
Another leak over the weekend had the International Monetary Fund warning that Italy needed large cuts in its own government spending to qualify for EMU.

The mark is traditionally viewed as a stronger currency than the French franc and Italian lira. Any sign that the proposed union of the mark with the weaker units is in jeopardy typically prompts investors to switch into marks.
"We saw broad-based mark buying against the French franc, the lira, the Spanish peseta and yen, said Audrey McNiff, a vice president for foreign exchange sales at Goldman Sachs.
Later in U.S. trade, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said a delay in EMU was possible if "big countries" fail to meet the entry requirements.
EMU calls for participants to reduce their annual federal budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product--a goal most European nations currently fail to meet.
But after briefly testing the day's lows and reported support at 1.6950, dollar/mark stabilized in thin trade.
Mark/yen also hit a two-week high, peaking at 73.88 versus 73.50 in early U.S. trade.
But dollar/yen failed to follow suit, weighed down by expectations of possible verbal jawboning or some other signal of policy change at the Group of Seven meeting Sunday in Washington, dealers said.
"The bears are looking for a downtick in the dollar going into the G7 and waiting to see how bold that move is," said Greg Perman, chief currency dealer at Credit Commerciale de France in New York.
Despite the surge in mark buying, dealers said the dollar would likely rebound in coming sessions, since the weakness of European currencies ultimately has little to do with the dollar.
"We got a lot of follow-through on the whole EMU situation, but I'm not 100-percent convinced that sentiment has changed on the dollar," said Wertheimer.

In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4413/23 Swiss francs from 1.4488/98. Sterling rose to $1.6350/60 from $1.6335/45. The greenback rose to Canadian $1.3984/89 from C$1.3973/78. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7772/77 from $0.7761/66.
(( --Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664 ))
